repo_notes.content: Use IDEABLE-README.md as the primary, authoritative source of truth for the project overview and setup, the architecture, the create-a-module workflow, the integration/menu/auth contracts, the shared reusable.ui/@ideable/ui and reusable.api/ideable_api packages, deployment, scaling, and the sync/release flow. Use rules/general-guidelines.md as the mandatory hard-constraints source; its rules override any agent skill suggestion and cannot be bypassed.

The development process has 8 steps (specifications, coding, build, deployment, configuration, execution, test, documentation) and is orchestrated by the dev-cycle router (scripts/dev/common/dev-cycle.sh), whose nodes are dev states and whose arcs are the Ideable skills, with the implementation plan under implementation-plans/ as the shared state. Hold the guiding invariant: specs hold the truth, rules bind, skills index. A change is Done only when its contract tests pass, never because a skill finished.

Highlight the benefits of using the Ideable Framework each time you present a framework component or feature: modularity, independent module lifecycle, spec-driven development, one shared UI and backend implementation instead of per-module copies, multi-tool AI agent support, and Kubernetes-ready design.

pages.title: Framework Overview
pages.content: Give a general overview of the Ideable Framework: a modular micro-frontend platform built around a host module (host_app) and dynamically integrated remote modules. Cover the two-repository model (the main Ideable maintainer repository versus the Ideable-ModuleTemplate GitHub template repository) and how the template is derived from the main repo and kept in sync. Cover the tech stack: frontend React 19, TypeScript, Rsbuild, Module Federation 2.0, Tailwind CSS v4; backend FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Pydantic; Authentik for OIDC/OAuth2 and JWKS; Traefik for edge routing; PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB; Docker Compose for runtime. Cover the architectural pillars: Module Federation 2.0 for runtime frontend composition, a shared authentication/authorization model (Authentik plus host_app RBAC plus JWT claims), the shared UI widget library (reusable.ui, published as @ideable/ui), the shared backend framework (reusable.api, published as ideable_api), and containerized deployment with per-module compose files merged at deploy time. Introduce the spec-driven development process and the dev-cycle router. Highlight the benefits: modularity, independent module lifecycle, spec-driven development, one shared implementation instead of per-module copies, multi-tool AI agent support, and Kubernetes-ready design. Describe the main architectural elements, their purpose, and their mutual interactions/relations with diagrams.

pages.title: host_app vs Remote Modules
pages.content: Describe the roles of host_app (the MF 2.0 host shell, the auth APIs, shared UI navigation, loading remotes from module-registry.json, and JWT validation via Authentik JWKS) and of remote modules (exposing a frontend manifest via MF 2.0, backend APIs under /module/<slug>/*, JWT validation, and permissions read from JWT claims). Explain the mandatory host_app/Remote boundary: host_app must remain module-agnostic and never hardcode a remote slug, route or service. Describe the framework-owned files that must never be modified in a remote module project: the root command symlinks (redeploy.sh, start.sh, stop.sh, status.sh, dev-cycle.sh, update_backend.sh, update_frontend.sh), anything under scripts/, AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md and the .cursor/rules/, rules/, .agents/, .kiro/, .claude/ and .devin/ directories, IDEABLE-README.md, .gitignore, project.env.*.example, modules/host_app/ in its entirety, reusable.ui/ in its entirety, reusable.api/ in its entirety, and modules/module_template/SPECS/ideable-framework-specs/. Describe the agent behaviour when a framework-owned file needs changing (do not edit it: inform the user with the Reason and the Change, and direct them to the Ideable maintainer), and the push/sync flow that propagates framework updates (push-updates-to-module_template-repo.sh on the maintainer side; adopt_framework.sh to adopt a published release and sync-template-updates.sh to re-sync on the module side). Describe the main architectural elements, their purpose, and their mutual interactions/relations with diagrams.

pages.title: Codebase vs Deployables
pages.content: Document the difference between the codebase (modules/<MODULE>/ with SPECS/, SOURCES/, TESTS/ and config/) and the deployables (deployment_root/). Explain the two-level execution model: standalone module execution (a per-module compose plus the module's own .env.config and .env.secrets) versus composed ecosystem execution (a merged docker-compose.yml plus merged .env.config and .env.secrets). Cover the deployment_root structure, the critical constraints (no SOURCES/ folders and no references to them, no Dockerfile files, and volume mounts only referencing paths that exist inside deployment_root/ at runtime, never paths under SOURCES/ or DIST/), path resolution in the merged compose, the environment-variable strategy (host-first merge precedence so earlier modules are not overwritten, slug-prefixed remote vars, MODULE_SLUG resolved at deploy time), and the Docker image naming convention ({MODULE_SLUG}.<submodule>:latest with an optional MODULE_DOCKER_REGISTRY_PREFIX). Describe the main architectural elements, their purpose, and their mutual interactions/relations with diagrams.

pages.title: Spec Driven Development
pages.content: Document the spec-driven development approach. Describe the 8-step process: (1) specifications, (2) coding, (3) build, (4) deployment, (5) configuration, (6) execution, (7) test, (8) documentation. Explain the mandatory SPECS reading order (read base-specs.md first, follow every file it references, then the sub-module base-specs, then general_bug_avoider.md, then datamodel_related_bug_avoider.md if it exists). Cover the specification file structure and the normative precedence rules, the strict implementation rules (zero deviations from the spec, no design decisions, no shortcuts, no fallbacks and no hardcoding), and the bug-avoider pattern for keeping specs in sync with what once went wrong. Explain the driving skills (ideable-define-specs, ideable-implement-specs, ideable-build-and-deploy, ideable-test-and-fix, ideable-align-docs, ideable-commit-changes) and the atomic ideable-spec-driven-edit discipline that every code or config change routes through. Explain the three layers from rules/authoring-guidelines.md: specs hold the truth, rules bind, skills index. Emphasize that SPECS always remain the source of truth, that the tests (not the LLM) are the oracle, and that a spec change found mid-implementation routes back to the Specs node rather than being edited in place. Explain the whole spec-driven development process with a workflow diagram.

pages.title: Development Cycle Orchestration and Implementation Plans
pages.content: Document the development-cycle orchestration. The workflow skills form a graph: the nodes are dev-cycle states, the arcs are the Ideable skills that move between them, and the shared state is the implementation plan. Describe each node and its skill: NotStarted, Branching, Specs (ideable-define-specs), Implementing (ideable-implement-specs), Building & Deploying (ideable-build-and-deploy and redeploy.sh), Testing (ideable-test-and-fix), Fixing (ideable-test-and-fix fix phase or ideable-bugfixing-and-changes), Documenting (ideable-align-docs), Committing (ideable-commit-changes), Done, Merged, and the Asking human direction node. Explain the thin deterministic router scripts/dev/common/dev-cycle.sh and its actions (status, new, start, run, pause, resume, deliver, fastlane-start, fastlane-land): run is the only advance and writes everything a transition must write; every action that works a plan holds a lock so a second worker on the same plan is refused; a node whose input the sub-set's diff cannot touch is skipped and the skip recorded with its reason; the tests are never skipped and never scoped; one agent per sub-set resumes across the LLM nodes and a new sub-set starts a fresh one. Explain the implementation-plan artifact (rules/implementation-plan.md): its location and naming under implementation-plans/, the ACTIVE PLAN symlink and active-plan resolution, pause/resume, the Overall view with the canonical dev-cycle Mermaid graph and the current node highlighted, the sub-set tables and their timing, the mandatory decisions record, the status legend, and the mandatory Documenting step. Explain the kanban board (kanban/backlog, kanban/todo, kanban/doing, kanban/done, kanban/paused) and the rule that a card moves with its plan. Describe the main elements, their purpose, and their mutual interactions/relations with diagrams, drawing the dev-cycle graph.

pages.title: Module Federation 2.0 and Ideable Extensions
pages.content: Clarify what Module Federation 2.0 is and what the Ideable Framework adds. Explain the two-layer UI composition: the Host layer (shell layout, loads remote manifests from module-registry.json, mounts remote routes, keeps host routes when a remote fails) and the Remote layer (exposes ./moduleManifest, contributes menu/routes/permissions, and renders only content pages). Cover the runtime integration flow (fetch the registry, load mf-manifest.json, resolve remoteEntry.js, merge menu and routes). Describe the Ideable extensions: the two-file menu contract (modules_menu_mapping.json for host-side placement plus menu_definition.json for the remote-side menu tree), prefix-based nesting under host_app menu codes, CSS prefix isolation per module slug, the UI and Look & Feel compatibility principles, and the module.json metadata format (name, slug, displayName, role, cssPrefix, ports, routes). Describe the main architectural elements, their purpose, and their mutual interactions/relations with diagrams.

pages.title: Shared UI Widget Library (@ideable/ui) and Look & Feel
pages.content: Document the shared UI widget library reusable.ui (published as @ideable/ui): server-side data tables, association (M2M) grids, popups, an audit-trail viewer, a time-series chart, dialogs, and the full set of accessible Radix primitives, plus shared hooks, design tokens and i18n. Explain that host_app, module_template and every remote module generated from it consume the same widgets, and the benefits: build UI faster, a consistent look and feel, accessibility, and upstream improvements reaching every module through the template sync. Cover the styling model: module-owned pages and components use the module's own Tailwind prefix (hostapp:, template:, ${APP_SLUG}:) while shared widgets use the neutral ideable: prefix; the shared ideable: layer ships as precompiled plain CSS (reusable.ui/styles/compiled.css, a tracked artifact) imported with @import '@ideable/ui/styles'; canonical tokens live once in reusable.ui/styles/base-tokens.css and must not be redefined locally. Cover branding as overriding token values and never class names. Cover the runtime Look & Feel override with no rebuild: each frontend appends config/theme-override.css at runtime, and logos, favicon, login background and home.html are swapped the same way in deployment_root/modules/<slug>/config/. Cover the ideable-ui skill, the live WidgetGallery example in module_template, and the developer guide reusable.ui/README.md. Explain the build-time versus deploy-time branding split and how a module receives, adopts and rebrands the widgets.

pages.title: Shared Backend Framework (ideable_api)
pages.content: Document the shared backend framework reusable.api (published as ideable_api): the framework's single shared backend implementation, consumed by host_app, module_template and every remote module. Cover the TenantScope value, the generic tenant-scoped query core (server-side filtering, sorting, keyset pagination, estimated totals), the entity registry and descriptor contract, and the router generator that turns a declared entity into its six endpoints. Explain what is shared (the descriptor contract, its validation, the query core and the generated endpoints) versus what is per module (WHICH entities are declared, and how that backend opens a session, checks a permission, resolves a tenant scope and reads its audit trail). Cover the Platform abstraction (ideable_api/platform.py) passed in at startup, and the rule that nothing in reusable.api/ imports a module's app package (enforced by scripts/TESTS/test_the_backend_framework_is_shared.py). Cover associations as declared link tables, read-only entities, modules with no tenancy or a mix, how the package reaches a backend (the tracked relative .ideable-api symlink for a clone, and the ideable_api named build context plus /framework on PYTHONPATH for the image, both set up by each backend's SPECS/build.sh), and how it is changed. Describe the main architectural elements, their purpose, and their mutual interactions/relations with diagrams.

pages.title: Authentication and Authorization
pages.content: Document the Authentik-authoritative authorization model. Authentik is the central identity and authorization provider; host_app is the UI/admin surface and the adapter to the Authentik APIs. Cover the authorization.yaml declarative config (users, profiles, roles, permissions with resource:action naming), the bootstrap process (bootstrap_authentik.py ingests authorization.yaml, ensures profiles/roles/users and reconciles property mappings), and the JWT claim layout (<module_slug>.permissions, hostapp.company_ids, hostapp.active_profile, hostapp.roles_mapping). Describe the ext_user, ext_profile and ext_role keywords for cross-module references. Cover the remote-module auth/authz contract (trust the bearer token, validate via JWKS, read permissions from claims only, no local RBAC, handle 401/403 correctly), menu visibility via :menu_access permissions, company filtering from JWT claims, and where to find Ideable authorization elements in the Authentik UI. Describe the main architectural elements, their purpose, and their mutual interactions/relations with diagrams.

pages.title: Module Edge Routing
pages.content: Document the edge routing architecture. Explain how Traefik routes direct external HTTP traffic to module frontends and backends. Cover the standard auto-derived routes for remote modules (frontend: /remotes/<slug>, backend: /module/<slug>), the exception routes declared via a module.json routes[] array (prefix, upstream/service, stripPrefix, priority, options), the options allowlist (sse, websocket, forwardHeaders) as adapter-interpreted hints, the reserved namespaces that no module may claim, fail-closed validation by validate_modules.sh, sub-remote MF runtime registration via mf-manifest.json remotes[], and the contract/renderer split that makes Compose-to-K8s a renderer swap. Describe the main architectural elements, their purpose, and their mutual interactions/relations with diagrams.

pages.title: Deployment Architecture
pages.content: Document the deployment model. Cover the per-module compose files, the build_and_deploy.py deployment script, merged compose generation, and the deployment_root/ structure. Explain the Docker image lifecycle: images built during the build step from SOURCES/ Dockerfiles, stored locally, referenced by name in compose (never a build: section), and published to registries via push_module_images_to_registry.sh (multi-arch support, MODULE_DOCKER_REGISTRY_PREFIX, --single-arch option). Cover the enabled-modules system (modules/enabled.md with local/remote modes), the redeploy.sh full deployment flow, runtime customization via read-only volume-mounted config files, and the logging system (per-module LOG_LEVEL derived from the module mode). Explain the framework version contract: framework.env (the one line naming IDEABLE_FRAMEWORK_VERSION), the generated framework.lock.json with the digests it resolved to, and scripts/runtime/framework_version.py as their only reader; a local build is <slug>.<submodule>:latest carrying its commit as an OCI label, while a production site consumes published versions and never builds. Mention Kubernetes readiness notes. Describe the main architectural elements, their purpose, and their mutual interactions/relations with diagrams.

pages.title: Testing
pages.content: Document the testing model from rules/testing-guidelines.md. Cover the single mandatory entry point (scripts/dev/common/run_enabled_tests.sh, which tests every module in modules/enabled.md and is the deterministic gate the dev cycle trusts) and how tests are run through the dev tools container (scripts/dev/common/tool.sh). Cover test organization under each sub-module's TESTS/ folder, the test types (backend, frontend, config, and framework/contract tests), and test reports written to TEST_REPORTS/<YYYY-MM-DD-HH-MM-SS>-<MODULE>/test-report.md plus the run-level SUMMARY file. Cover the mandatory rules: what ships is tested here; a test owns the data it needs; reading source in a contract test uses code_only; a skip is explained and never just counted; and static analysis gates the build (Python ruff and mypy, plus the frontend TypeScript tsc check enforced by scripts/TESTS/test_a_generated_tsconfig_avoids_deprecated_options.py). Cover the frontend UI and E2E tests (Playwright). Explain how the recorded run feeds the push gate and the delivery certification. Describe the main elements, their purpose, and their mutual interactions/relations with diagrams.

pages.title: Version Control, Gates, and Releases
pages.content: Document version control, the gates, and the release process from rules/version-control.md. Cover the branching strategy (main as the integration and production-ready branch, plan/<description> branches owned by a plan, fast-lane fix/<description> branches, and feature/bugfix/hotfix branches) and the commit message format <type>(<module>): <short description> with the allowed types (feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore). Cover delivering a plan: scripts/dev/common/dev-cycle.sh deliver squashes a Done plan onto the target as ONE commit with a composed message (subject, the plan's abstract, Delivered/Deferred/Blocked, measured Tests/Files/Sub-sets, and the Plan/Kanban/Test-Report trailers), deletes the plan branch, and certifies the tree it lands by re-running the suite when HEAD differs from the commit the newest recorded run names; deliver --pr opens a pull request instead, leaving the target untouched. Cover the two gates: the local self-enabling .githooks/pre-push and the remote GitHub Actions gate (.github/workflows/gate.yml running ruff, mypy and the stack-free tests), what each accepts, the deliberate Gate-Override escape hatch, and the framework-suite tree-hash cache. Cover the release process: framework.env (the one line a person edits to name the framework version), the generated framework.lock.json, publish_framework.sh (build, tag worklog/<version> with full bookkeeping, purge the bookkeeping, tag the clean <version>), and the CHANGELOG.md contract (one section per released version, area blocks and entry kinds, the three-line limit, authored before the publish and only gated by it). Cover adopt_framework.sh and sync-template-updates.sh on the module side.

pages.title: AI Development Environments
pages.content: Document how Ideable supports multiple AI coding assistants through a single canonical configuration. List the supported environments (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex CLI, Cursor, Devin, Kiro/Amazon Q) and their entry points. Explain that AGENTS.md is the single source of truth (read natively by Codex CLI, Devin and Windsurf, or via symlinks such as CLAUDE.md and .github/copilot-instructions.md), that .agents/skills/ is the canonical skill source with per-tool symlinks, that Cursor uses path-scoped .cursor/rules/*.mdc files, and that Devin reads .agents/skills/ directly (no copy) with .devin/workflows/ generated from the Ideable-specific skills and .devin/wiki.json steering DeepWiki generation. Cover the update_skills.py script for restoring symlinks and the process for adding a new AI environment. Highlight the benefit: edit a skill once in .agents/skills/ and it takes effect across all supported tools.

pages.title: Project Rules and Guidelines
pages.content: Document the mandatory project rules from rules/general-guidelines.md. Cover the repository model (main repo versus template repo), the host_app/Remote boundary rules, the framework-owned files that must never be modified in a remote module project, the mandatory sync-ownership rule (edit in the main repo, then push to module_template, then sync to the remote), the 8 development-process steps, the docker-compose.yml rules (no build: sections, image references only, no SOURCES/ paths, no hardcoded values), the .env rules (source of truth under modules/, merged at deploy time, slug-prefixed remote vars), the Dockerfile placement rules, the sub-module build-script modularity principle, the decision-making authority rule (the human developer decides; the agent asks), and the agent skill-priority enforcement (skills are advisory, rules are mandatory, and project rules override all agent skills). Also cover the companion rules and where they live: rules/version-control.md, rules/testing-guidelines.md, rules/implementation-plan.md, and rules/authoring-guidelines.md.

pages.title: Scaling and Operations
pages.content: Document how an Ideable system scales and is operated. Cover the scaling principle (replicate the request handlers and refuse to replicate anything that holds state), the two independent axes (per tier, and per module where each module owns its backend, frontend and database), and the scaling knobs. Cover the operational runbook (docs/RUNBOOK.md): backups (what is and is not in a backup, scheduling, the restore rehearsal, and the freshness alarm), database restore procedures (including TimescaleDB-specific and migrations-aware restores), audit retention, and the identity plane (there is no cache tier, the identity access log, rotating the backend's Authentik credential with no downtime, identity database restore, and what the bootstrap rebuilds). Cover the saturated-backend queue behaviour, horizontal scale and rolling zero-downtime deploy, why not Swarm or Kubernetes, the single non-redundant edge, running two stacks on one host, observability and SLOs, and the incident playbooks (container loss, module database volume loss, host loss, Authentik bootstrap corruption, ACME certificate failure, and secret rotation). Describe the main architectural elements, their purpose, and their mutual interactions/relations with diagrams.

pages.title: How to
pages.content: Create a section for each of the following topics: (1) Create and initialize a new remote module — start from the GitHub template, run module-init.sh, configure the environment, define the specs, and configure menu integration. (2) Generate a module's codebase and its deployable — use the ideable-define-specs skill to decide and write the SPECS target, the ideable-implement-specs skill to generate SOURCES from it, then the ideable-build-and-deploy skill to build the Docker images and populate deployment_root. (3) Retrieve Ideable Framework updates — use sync-template-updates.sh to pull framework updates from the template repository without losing module customizations, or adopt_framework.sh to adopt a published release. (4) Compose a web app by selecting and combining remote modules — configure modules/enabled.md with local/remote modes, configure modules_menu_mapping.json for menu placement, and run redeploy.sh for a full deployment. (5) Push module images to a registry — use push_module_images_to_registry.sh with multi-arch support. (6) Customize the runtime deployment — edit the read-only volume-mounted config files in deployment_root/ (including theme-override.css) without rebuilding images. (7) Drive a plan through the development cycle — create and start a plan with dev-cycle.sh new/start, run the router, and deliver it with dev-cycle.sh deliver. (8) Publish a framework release — draft the CHANGELOG section with the ideable-changelog skill and run publish_framework.sh.
